notes: Method: WebSearch (extended) to locate vendor pages, then WebFetch; where WebFetch and plain curl were refused (Empower, Monarch: HTTP 403), the Zendesk Help Center public JSON endpoint (/api/v2/help_center/<locale>/articles/<id>.json) returned the same articles and the quotes were taken from their body text (tags stripped; runs of inline-formatted words are joined with single spaces). Patterns across products relevant to Bagholder: (1) every tracker that handles debt stores it as a balance on a Liability-typed account and shows one net worth total (Empower, Monarch, Kubera, Wealthica, Wealthsimple, Ghostfolio); only Kubera visually pairs each debt with the asset it secures. (5) Pure portfolio trackers (Sharesight, Snowball, Delta, Portfolio Performance) do not model liabilities at all. claims.quote: The interest is an expense representing the cost of borrowing, and thus of having, the car and the education.

verdict.why: The page was fetched and the quoted sentence appears verbatim, in the paragraph: "Each loan payment actually covers the interest expense and partial repayment of the loan. The interest is an expense representing the cost of borrowing, and thus of having, the car and the education. The repayment of the loan is not an expense, however, but is just giving back something that was borrowed." So the substance of the claim (interest on a loan is an expense, the cost of borrowing; principal repayment is not an expense) is supported. One imprecision: the page makes this distinction in its income-statement discussion, not specifically in its cash-flow treatment; on the cash flow statement the page classes the loan repayments (car and education) as cash flows from financing, and it does not separately say how interest is placed on the cash flow statement. The page discusses car and student loans only; mortgages are not mentioned.
verdict.page_says_instead: Interest is an expense (included on the income statement); loan principal repayment is not an expense and is excluded from the income statement. On the cash flow statement, loan repayments appear as cash flows from financing. The "expense" characterisation is an income-statement point rather than a cash-flow-statement point.
